rv.q: Within this gimmickry, Threlfall delivers a fairly classic Lear, deeply affecting in the deathbed scenes but, having established the character’s nationalism, winning a big laugh with the usually nothing line, “Am I in France ?”
This is a King Lear that is a truly gripping masterpiece.
For a city that prides itself on doing things differently, this is a brilliantly alternative take on the work.
Overall, I'm not sure what to think.
Threlfall delivers the monarch in all his terrible, heartbreaking glory but this is a production that promises so much but never quite matches his stature.
It is an astonishing performance and quite possibly the work of a lifetime.
Dunster’s King Lear feels cinematic and epic in scale, taking you through a range of emotions without losing its uncomfortable relevance.
King Lear is a thrilling anniversary production that makes the most of everything the Royal Exchange does so well.
With outstanding performances, striking staging and moments that are both moving and genuinely shocking, King Lear is a powerful production that certainly leaves a lasting impression.
Overall, King Lear is a powerful, thought-provoking night at the theatre, anchored by Threlfall ’s compelling performance and a story that proves some family problems really are timeless.
A blistering performance, Dunster’s King Lear is as powerful in its meandering monologues as in its vivid bloodshed and violence.
A powerful and visually spectacular evening at the theatre, with outstanding performances and some genuinely unforgettable moments.
This is a missed opportunity to reimagine Lear at a time when the world is literally burning.

In a year of notable Lears – including Maureen Beattie’s superb, feminised monarch in Pitlochry and Ian McDiarmid’s memorable playing in Sheffield – the impressive David Threlfall is let down by a frustratingly uneven production at the Royal Exchange in Manchester.
The promotional material for King Lear sees the "King" scribbled out, which captures the problem with this adaptation: Lear has been denied his crowning glory.

cn.t: Threlfall delivers a compelling, emotionally powerful Lear in Dunster's bold, visually striking production, though critics are divided on the adaptation's unconventional choices and uneven supporting performances.
